The page does not list compile flags (they are only implicit in the public Makefile, -O3 by default), so B as in earlier lzbench-based verdicts, not A.
notes: All README (Ryzen 9 9950X) and lzbench numbers in the record match the pages exactly. In the README table kanzi -l 7 (1150 ms, 47,330,431 B) also beats zstd 1.6.0 -T16 -19 (11090 ms, 52,830,213 B) on both speed and size; the decompression of kanzi at high levels is slower than xz in lzbench, as the record already says.

notes: All numbers in the record match the README and lzbench pages. tier_reason: A peer-reviewed ACM HPDC 2023 paper (opened as the PDF checked into mxmlnkn/indexed_bzip2) reports 5.6 GB/s on Silesia, a speedup of 33 over GNU gzip, and 8.7 GB/s on base64 data, a speedup of 55 over gzip and 21 over igzip, on 2x AMD EPYC 7702. Neither the paper nor the README states the compiler or flags, so not A.

corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed (ACM HPDC 2023, DOI 10.1145/3588195.3592992); the paper PDF in mxmlnkn/indexed_bzip2/results/paper was opened, but neither it nor the README states the compiler or flags. The headline gain is parallel scaling versus single-threaded GNU gzip, not a faster single-thread inflate: in the paper (rapidgzip 0.5.0), single-threaded rapidgzip reached 153 MB/s, while bgzip was 1.9x and igzip 4.3x as fast; the README's claim that single-core speed is close to igzip refers to later versions. Baseline is GNU gzip rather than zlib. The README scaling plots used rapidgzip 0.9.0, and its values are higher than the paper's. The paper's text gives GNU gzip on Silesia as "172 GB/s", an evident typo for MB/s.

notes: README Ryzen 3900X tables match the record exactly (5640 MB/s vs gzip 293 MB/s, 18.8x with index; 2070 MB/s, 6.9x from scratch; base64 5060 vs 250 MB/s, 20.1x). Last commit 2025-11-30 (v0.16.0), within 12 months, so active. The repo page lists Apache-2.0 and MIT; the per-file split was not checked.
